investigation_type: Discovery; conflict reconstruction; dispatcher judgment; policy selection; complexity test; residual arbitration test

presentation.investigation_summary:
Field-service scheduling complexity, competing objectives, changing conditions, policy variation, and human exceptions are real. Current ServiceNow evidence shows policies, weighted objectives, hard/soft constraints, dynamic and intraday optimization, policy switching, contextual overrides, preferred technicians, appointment overrides, and manual exceptions. The proposed recurring material policy-arbitration burden was not established.

1. Field-service exceptions may expose a new decision domain.
2. Real conflicts and multi-objective dispatcher judgment were verified.
3. The hypothesis narrowed to context-dependent policy selection and then policy explosion/arbitration.
4. Native capability testing showed the platform can encode objectives, constraints, policies, dynamic reoptimization, context variation, and human override.
5. **Final:** recurring material customer burden and ServiceNow-specific gap remain NOT ESTABLISHED. **KILL.**

key_findings.statement: Multi-skill, multi-objective field-service scheduling — Underlying complexity is real.
Policies, objectives, weights, and constraints — Core decision representation is native.
Dynamic and intraday optimization — Changing conditions are supported.
Dispatcher-selected policy and contextual overrides — Policy adaptation is supported.
Manual exception and preference mechanisms — Human involvement is designed into the workflow.
Policy explosion, recurring error, material loss — Residual opportunity fails.

decision.decision: **KILL OPP-006.** Do not create another field-service checkpoint or convert it to AIL. Start a new decision domain.
decision.reason:
Field-service scheduling complexity, competing objectives, changing conditions, policy variation, and human exceptions are real. Current ServiceNow evidence shows policies, weighted objectives, hard/soft constraints, dynamic and intraday optimization, policy switching, contextual overrides, preferred technicians, appointment overrides, and manual exceptions. The proposed recurring material policy-arbitration burden was not established.

KILL reflects an evidence failure at the residual opportunity boundary, not a claim that field-service complexity or human judgment is unreal.

primary_question:
Whether complex field-service context creates recurring human policy-selection burden beyond finite policies, objectives, constraints, overrides, and optimization

The investigation began by searching a new business decision domain after OPP-005. The initial hypothesis was that field-service exceptions might require intelligence beyond native scheduling. After real conflicts were found, it narrowed to whether dispatchers face recurring policy-arbitration burden that cannot be encoded economically.

Microsoft's official customer story for Ausgrid provides unusually direct evidence of a field-service scheduling conflict.
Ausgrid describes a situation where schedulers needed to dispatch an urgent unplanned job but could not see the planned work already assigned to field technicians.
Source:
https://www.microsoft.com/en/customers/story/25279-ausgrid-dynamics-365-field-service
The documented problem was:
PLANNED FIELD WORK
+
URGENT UNPLANNED JOB
↓
SCHEDULER CANNOT SEE BOTH
↓
PRIORITIZATION FAILURE
↓
HIGH-PRIORITY JOBS COULD BE CANCELLED UNWITTINGLY
↓
CANCELLED WORK WAITED WEEKS FOR RESCHEDULING
↓
PRODUCTIVITY / EFFICIENCY IMPACT
↓
CUSTOMER COMMITMENT IMPACT
Source:
https://www.microsoft.com/en/customers/story/25279-ausgrid-dynamics-365-field-service

This is materially stronger than generic claims such as:
> "Field-service schedules change frequently."
The source describes an actual operational conflict:
EXISTING PLANNED WORK
VS
URGENT NEW WORK
The problem was not simply lack of scheduling.
It was inability to see the competing commitments together before making the dispatch decision.
The documented consequence was that high-priority jobs could be cancelled unintentionally, with cancelled work taking weeks to reschedule.
Source:
https://www.microsoft.com/en/customers/story/25279-ausgrid-dynamics-365-field-service

The documented initial state was:
TECHNICIANS
↓
PLANNED WORK ALREADY ASSIGNED
Then:
URGENT UNPLANNED JOB
↓
DISPATCH REQUIRED
The scheduler needed to decide how to accommodate the urgent job without destroying already-planned work.
But the scheduling information was fragmented.
### Initial decision problem
KEEP PLANNED WORK
VS
PRIORITIZE URGENT WORK
The organization could not reliably evaluate both sides because scheduling information was not visible across systems.

The documented consequence was severe enough to matter operationally:
- high-priority jobs could be cancelled unintentionally;
- cancelled work could take weeks to reschedule;
- productivity and efficiency were affected;
- customer promises were at risk.
Source:
https://www.microsoft.com/en/customers/story/25279-ausgrid-dynamics-365-field-service
This establishes:
DECISION FAILURE
↓
SCHEDULE DISRUPTION
↓
REWORK / RESCHEDULING
↓
CUSTOMER CONSEQUENCE

provenance.section: 23. What the Real Evidence Actually Reveals

evidence.statement:
A peer-reviewed research article, *Focusing on Customer Time in Field Service: A Normative Approach*, explicitly studies the trade-off between customer convenience and field-service provider cost.
Source:
https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1937-5956.2007.tb00175.x
The paper states that customer convenience should be central to field-service operations and investigates the explicit inclusion of customer time in nonemergency field-service decisions together with the trade-off between customer convenience and provider cost.

provenance.section: 3. Strongest External Evidence — Customer Time vs Provider Cost

evidence.statement:
This is stronger than simply saying field-service scheduling has multiple objectives.
It establishes a genuine business trade-off:
CUSTOMER CONVENIENCE
VS
PROVIDER COST
A schedule can therefore be operationally feasible while still producing different business outcomes.

A peer-reviewed open-access study in *Computers & Operations Research* describes field-service scheduling as involving multiple objectives including:
- cost;
- task priorities;
- consumer satisfaction.
Source:
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cor.2021.105472
The study describes a two-level optimization approach in which tasks are assigned to time intervals and then precisely scheduled and routed.

A published study on data-driven field-service planning reports that dispatchers struggle with multiple competing objectives including:
- technician utilization;
- response time;
- customer satisfaction.
Source:
https://www.researchgate.net/publication/333718957_Redesigning_Service_Operations_for_the_Digital_World_Towards_Automated_and_Data-driven_Field_Service_Planning
The study describes approaches that consolidate competing objectives into an optimization problem and support dynamic rescheduling when conditions change.

provenance.section: 7. Industry Evidence — Dispatchers Face Competing Objectives

evidence.statement:
The same research points toward optimization rather than an unavoidable human-reasoning bottleneck.
The documented approach is:
COMPETING OBJECTIVES
↓
FORMALIZE OBJECTIVES
↓
OPTIMIZATION
↓
DYNAMIC RESCHEDULING
Therefore:
> **The existence of competing objectives does not itself establish the need for a separate reasoning layer.**

ServiceNow's current Schedule Optimization explicitly separates:
### Objectives
Soft goals that influence which schedule is preferred.
### Constraints
Hard rules that an assignment must satisfy.
Source:
https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/field-service-management/hard-soft-constraints.html
ServiceNow states that objectives are weighted, with higher weights receiving greater priority.
Source:
https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/field-service-management/hard-soft-constraints.html

ServiceNow allows both:
MINIMIZE SLA VIOLATION
+
MINIMIZE OVERTIME
to be configured as objectives.
Source:
https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/field-service-management/hard-soft-constraints.html
The optimization policy can assign weights to objectives.
Source:
https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/field-service-management/field-service-scheduling/create-policies-schedule-optimization.html

ServiceNow provides an intraday objective:
**Maximize existing assignments**
It also provides objectives for high-priority work and delayed tasks.
Source:
https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/field-service-management/hard-soft-constraints.html
This means a conflict can already be expressed approximately as:
PRESERVE CURRENT SCHEDULE
VS
ACCOMMODATE NEW PRIORITY
through configured objectives.

A current 2026 field-service implementation article discussing Microsoft Dynamics 365 Resource Scheduling Optimization reports that optimization handles complex combinations of resources, rules and goals, but that strict rules can produce no feasible result and users may find it difficult to understand why a technician was reassigned or why work was postponed.
Source:
https://promx.net/en/2026/05/hands-on-hands-off-from-manual-dispatching-to-system-driven-scheduling-in-dynamics-365-field-service/
The article identifies a tension:
STRONG AUTOMATION
↓
CONSISTENT RULE EXECUTION
VS
OPERATIONAL TRANSPARENCY

Source:
https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/field-service-management/field-service-scheduling/create-policies-schedule-optimization.html

ServiceNow's current documentation goes further.
Its on-demand optimization documentation explicitly states:
> Dispatchers can change the policy before running optimization to adapt to current conditions.
Source:
https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/field-service-management/field-service-scheduling/configure-on-demand-optimization.html

https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/field-service-management/field-service-scheduling/configure-on-demand-optimization.html

provenance.section: 6. Native Evidence — Policy as Business Rules
7. Native Evidence — Current Conditions Can Trigger Reoptimization

evidence.statement:
Salesforce provides unusually explicit documentation of the same operational pattern.
Its field-service scheduling documentation describes multiple policies for different scenarios.
Examples include:
- Customer First;
- High Intensity;
- Soft Boundaries;
- Emergency.
The documentation explicitly states that dispatchers select different scheduling policies as the situation changes.
Source:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/field-service-lightning-scheduling-basics/customize-a-scheduling-policy
### Example documented scenario
An emergency such as a local power outage can require rescheduling appointments in a territory.
The documented response is to select a different scheduling policy.
Source:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/field-service-lightning-scheduling-basics/customize-a-scheduling-policy

Salesforce's documented pattern is:
NORMAL DAY
↓
CUSTOMER-FIRST POLICY
↓
OPERATING CONDITIONS CHANGE
↓
EMERGENCY / HIGH VOLUME
↓
POLICY SHIFT
↓
EMERGENCY / HIGH-INTENSITY POLICY
↓
REOPTIMIZE
Source:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/field-service-lightning-scheduling-basics/customize-a-scheduling-policy

This proves that:
> **Context-dependent policy selection is a real field-service operating pattern.**
It is not merely a theoretical AI workflow.
It also demonstrates that mature field-service platforms can implement the pattern without a specialized reasoning engine.

A PG&E utility procedure provides a more operationally concrete example.
The documented procedure covers Priority Zero gas field orders.
When an emergency field order is dispatched to personnel already working on non-priority work, the dispatcher may reschedule or reassign the non-emergency work.
When an emergency order is dispatched to personnel working on a customer-generated field order, the dispatcher may reassign the customer order if necessary.
Source:
https://www.phmsa.dot.gov/sites/phmsa.dot.gov/files/docs/standards-rulemaking/pipeline/interpretations/77451/pge-and-local-1245-pi-23-0001-04-06-2023-part199-1.pdf

A published decision-support study addresses real-time field-service engineer scheduling with emergencies and collaboration.
It describes emergency levels and policies for repair jobs and uses event-driven replanning and rescheduling.
Source:
https://www.researchgate.net/publication/290471804_Decision_Support_System_for_a_Real-Time_Field_Service_Engineer_Scheduling_Problem_with_Emergencies_and_Collaborations

Across ServiceNow documentation, Salesforce documentation, utility procedures, and academic field-service research, the following pattern is supported:
OPERATING CONTEXT
↓
EVENT / CONDITION CHANGE
↓
CURRENT PRIORITY MODEL
MAY BECOME INAPPROPRIATE
↓
ALTERNATIVE POLICY / PRIORITY MODEL
↓
POLICY SELECTION
↓
REOPTIMIZATION / DISPATCH

This is where the evidence becomes decisive.
ServiceNow automatically responds to many scheduling disruptions.
